newsitem.title: USA: American Greetings may seek UK buy - CEO.
newsitem.headline: American Greetings may seek UK buy - CEO.

text.p: American Greetings Corp may seek acquisitions in the British Isles, chairman and chief executive officer Morry Weiss said Tuesday.

"We need to strengthen our market share position (in the British Isles) so it might very well be that possible additional acquisitions in the United Kingdom might be the right thing for us," he said in a telephone interview.
The cardmaker has not targeted any candidates nor held any discussions, he stressed. It is comfortable with its market position elsewhere in the UK, he said.
It owns an Australia/New Zealand cardmaker, a Canada subsidiary and a majority interest in a South African firm.
American Greetings is the second largest cardmaker, after privately held Hallmark Cards Inc, based in Kansas City.

Hallmark is estimated to have more than 40 percent of the U.S. market. American Greetings has about one-third, Cincinnati-based Gibson Greetings Inc has less than 10 percent and smaller companies make up the rest.

Weiss said American Greetings is still interested in Gibson but only if Gibson initiates talks -- which, he said, seems unlikely. Gibson has said repeatedly it is not for sale. Last year it rejected an American Greetings offer.
In the year ended in February 1996, American Greetings had $2 billion revenues and operating income of $2.01 a share.
As reported, Weiss said Monday the company is on track to report earnings of $2.20-$2.25 a share for the current year.
Sales for Christmas, the number-one selling season, were "really good," Weiss said, and the Valentine's Day selling season, the number-two period, looks "phenomenal" so far.
Weiss said greeting cards account for about two-thirds of the company's sales and a "much larger" percent of profits. Greeting card profitability is "outstanding," Weiss said.

A few years ago the card business was thought to be mature and slow-growing, but Weiss said American Greetings' sales and market share are growing because of its focus on selling its wares in mass retailers such as Kmart Corp, Wal-Mart Stores Inc, supermarkets and drugstores.
He said most cards today are sold in such outlets, not the specialty card shops where Hallmark traditionally focused.

With growing card sales and profits, Weiss said the company may consider selling one or two of its four units that make products other than individual cards -- photo frames, non-prescription eyeglasses, photo frames, hair accessories and seasonal boxed cards and giftwrap.
The units account for about 13 percent of sales, he said. All are profitable but some are performing below expectations and all are less profitable than greeting cards, he said.

Sally Schaadt, an analyst with the Fourteen Research Corp, said the eyeglass unit might be the most likely to be sold. The cardmaker last fall broke off talks to acquire sunglass maker Foster Grant Group from BEC Group saying it did not fit business objectives.
Weiss said it has not identified which units, if any, to sell. The company's stock closed up 1 at 28-5/8 on Nasdaq.
